# Acids, alkalis and indicators (`acids_bases_ph`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: helped by alkali_soda, lime_burning
- Core idea: Acids (vinegar, lemon juice, the mineral acids) taste sour, make chalk fizz and dissolve many metals; alkalis (ash lye, soda, lime water, ammonia) feel soapy and attack fats. They destroy each other's properties, giving a salt and water, and the amounts needed are always in the same proportion. Plant juices show which is which: syrup of violets or red cabbage water turns red with acid and green with alkali, litmus red and blue. With one solution of known concentration, the volume needed to reach a suitable indicator endpoint gives the concentration of the other. pH measures acidity on a logarithmic scale: a fall of one unit means ten times the hydrogen-ion activity.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking only acids burn; strong alkalis destroy skin and especially eyes more insidiously.
  - Neutralising a burn on the skin with the opposite chemical; rinse with much water instead.
  - Lavoisier's error that every acid contains oxygen. Hydrochloric acid has none; the common ingredient is hydrogen.
  - Equating 'strong' with 'concentrated', or judging an acid by taste.
- History: mesopotamia: 3rd millennium BC – vinegar and plant-ash alkali used in cleaning and dyeing; islamic: 8th–10th c. – alkalis (al-qali) and sharp waters classified by Jabirian authors and al-Razi; europe: c. 1300 – litmus from lichens (Arnald of Villanova); 1664 Boyle uses plant colours as indicators; 1750s Rouelle defines a base; 1810 Davy shows muriatic acid holds no oxygen; 1884 Arrhenius; 1909 Sørensen's pH scale; 1923 Brønsted and Lowry
- Read:
  - Robert Boyle, Experiments and Considerations Touching Colours (1664)
  - William H. Brock, The Fontana History of Chemistry (1992)
